prompt.context: Our client is a 350-bed hospital in a mid-size city. The organization has historically exhibited strong financial performance, and had a 1-3% operating gain each year for the last five years. However, they are projecting a $12 million operating loss this year, and expect this situation to worsen in the future. As a result, the CFO believes that they will be out of cash within five years. They are one of the largest employers in the market, and will not consider layoffs as a possible solution.
prompt.question: They have asked us to identify the source of this sudden downturn, and to come up with alternatives to restore them to a break-even position.

clarifying_info.a: Revenues have dropped approximately 15% so far this year due to aggressive pricing on capitated managed care contracts signed in January, and declining admissions and length of stay for fee-for-service contracts (most reimbursed on a per diem basis). All contracts are binding for three years and cannot be renegotiated.

clarifying_info.q: What is the hospital's occupancy and cost structure?
clarifying_info.a: Hospital occupancy is approximately 70%, resulting in high fixed costs not covered by the current contribution margin. The organization is currently staffed for 80% occupancy.

clarifying_info.q: Are there issues with resource utilization during patient stays?
clarifying_info.a: The utilization of diagnostic and therapeutic services during a patient's stay is approximately 15% higher than what was expected when contract pricing was negotiated.

clarifying_info.q: What does the local competitive market look like?
clarifying_info.a: There are two other 350-bed hospitals in the city: one is an academic medical center, the other a Catholic hospital recently acquired by a for-profit chain. Additionally, total admissions in the marketplace have dropped by 5% and total patient days have declined 10%.

framework: Revenue: analyze contract types (capitated managed care vs. fee-for-service), pricing, volume (admissions, length of stay)
Costs: break into fixed vs. variable; fixed costs tied to staffing levels and capacity; variable costs driven by resource utilization per patient stay
Generate alternatives: (1) cost reduction levers given the no-layoff constraint, and (2) revenue enhancement strategies
Consider competitive/market dynamics and strategic options such as affiliation or consolidation

questions.prompt: What is driving the revenue decline?
questions.guidance: Revenues fell ~15% due to: (1) aggressively priced capitated managed care contracts signed in January — capitated contracts pay a fixed amount per member regardless of utilization, so underpricing hurts directly; (2) declining admissions and shorter lengths of stay on fee-for-service contracts reimbursed on a per diem basis. All contracts are locked in for three years and cannot be renegotiated, so revenue is fixed in the near term.

questions.prompt: What is the cost challenge given the revenue situation?
questions.guidance: Occupancy is ~70% but staffing is set for 80% occupancy, creating a mismatch: high fixed costs that are not covered by the current contribution margin. Since the hospital will not consider layoffs, the fixed cost base is difficult to reduce quickly. Candidate should recognize that variable cost management becomes the primary lever.

questions.prompt: What variable cost levers are available?
questions.guidance: Staffing is the largest variable cost but is off the table (no layoffs). The remaining key driver is resource utilization per patient stay, which is running ~15% above the level assumed when contracts were priced. This over-utilization directly erodes the margin on capitated contracts. Candidates should identify physician behavior as the root cause of utilization.

questions.prompt: How can the hospital reduce costs given the no-layoff constraint?
questions.guidance: Focus on physician-driven resource utilization: (1) Align MD incentives with hospital economics by sharing risk or offering performance-based compensation; (2) Provide physicians with data and benchmarking on their resource use versus peers and competitors; (3) Sign exclusive contracts with a single distributor to generate volume discounts and purchasing economies; (4) Limit the pharmacy formulary to generics; (5) Reduce vendor choice for high-volume items such as prosthetics and heart catheters.

questions.prompt: How can the hospital increase revenue?
questions.guidance: (1) Sign contracts with additional insurers to broaden the payor mix; (2) Employ salaried physicians to guarantee admissions to the hospital; (3) Create an affiliated physician organization to increase share of admissions; (4) Develop Centers of Excellence (distinctive clinical competencies) that can be marketed to managed care contractors as an exclusive regional or supra-regional provider, enabling premium pricing.

Given market context — two other 350-bed hospitals, a 5% admissions decline, and a 10% drop in patient days — consolidation or affiliation should be considered. Affiliating with a competitor could rationalize service lines across institutions, potentially allow one hospital to close, reduce total market capacity, and lower fixed costs across the system.

brainstorming.prompt: What solutions exist to restore the hospital to break-even?

categories.name: Cost Reduction
ideas: Align physician incentives with hospital cost goals (risk-sharing, performance pay)
Provide physicians with comparative utilization data and education
Sign exclusive distributor contracts for volume discounts
Limit pharmacy formulary to generic drugs
Reduce vendor count for high-volume supplies (prosthetics, catheters)

categories.name: Revenue Enhancement
ideas: Sign contracts with additional insurers to expand payor mix
Hire salaried physicians to guarantee hospital admissions
Form an affiliated physician organization to capture more admissions
Develop Centers of Excellence marketed as exclusive regional providers to managed care contractors

categories.name: Strategic / Market Options
ideas: Affiliate with or acquire a competitor to rationalize market capacity
Pursue managed closure of one hospital to reduce city-wide fixed costs
Explore merger with the for-profit-acquired Catholic hospital or the academic medical center

recommendation: In the near term, the hospital cannot change its revenue contracts; therefore, the primary lever is reducing variable costs by targeting the 15% excess resource utilization through physician engagement programs (risk-sharing, benchmarking data, education) and supply chain consolidation (exclusive distributor deals, formulary restriction, vendor reduction).

In the medium term, the hospital should pursue revenue growth by expanding its payor base, employing physicians to secure admissions, and building Centers of Excellence to win exclusive managed care contracts at premium rates.

Strategically, given a market-wide admissions decline and three hospitals of similar size, the hospital should explore affiliation or consolidation to rationalize capacity and reduce the fixed cost burden across the city.
risks: Physician resistance to incentive realignment or behavioral change programs may slow cost reduction
Market consolidation or affiliation negotiations are complex and may not close within the five-year cash runway
Revenue growth initiatives (new contracts, Centers of Excellence) take time to generate material income
next_steps: Conduct physician utilization benchmarking and design a risk-sharing incentive model
Audit supply chain spend and identify top candidates for exclusive contracts and formulary restriction
Map the competitive landscape to identify the best potential affiliation or merger partner
Model the financial impact of each initiative against the $12M operating loss target
